newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax plan sees big cuts, but VAT undecided.
newsitem.headline: German tax plan sees big cuts, but VAT undecided.

text.p: The tax reform scheme hammered out by Germany's ruling coalition would slash income and corporate taxes while scrapping a slew of tax breaks, but the thorny issue of hiking value-added tax remained open on Thursday.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking after marathon talks on Wednesday, hailed the two-stage reform plan as the biggest in Germany's post-war history.

Although Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he was "very satisfied" with the proposal, it is far from a done deal. Party leaders in Kohl's tripartite alliance were reviewing the proposal before its unveiling later today by Waigel.
Details of the compromise obtained by Reuters showed that the tax shakeup -- to take effect in two steps in 1998 and 1999 -- would slash 81.9 billion marks in taxes.
Scrapping tax breaks to broaden the tax base would bring in an extra 38.1 billion marks to compensate. Simple arithmetic yields net tax cuts overall of 43.8 billion marks.
But that is more than the government can afford, and Waigel has said the outstanding amount would have to be financed by an increase in VAT to bring the net reduction down to 30 billion.

The tax reform is being touted as a panacea for Germany's unemployment-hit economy, but has already run into criticism from opposition parties which say it punishes those on middle and low incomes while offering giveaways to the rich.
The reform package is "a mixture of reform, retouches and tricks," Joachim Poss, finance spokesman of the Social Democrats (SPD) told German Radio.
Poss attacked the plan's 15 percent starting rate, which he said would be levied on incomes too low to tax. "It violates the principle not to tax at the poverty level," he said.
The proposals seem almost as complicated as Germany's tax system -- which is so labyrinthine that it has generated a huge tax consulting industry and two-thirds of world tax literature.
The main points look like this: Incomes below 13,000 marks for single earners would be tax-free from 1999. Pay up to 18,000 marks would be taxed at 15 percent.
Then, a sliding scale running from 22.5 percent comes into force, hitting a top rate of 39 percent at 90,000 marks.
The new income tax rates, to take effect in 1999, would cut existing rates running from 26 percent to 53 percent and bring the lion's share of the tax cuts at 69.1 billion marks.
The other big tax cut would be a two-step drop in corporate taxation. From 1999, retained profits would be taxed at 35 percent and profits distributed to shareholders at 25 percent.
That's the simple part. A coalition document listed over 70 items designed to boost state revenues by abolishing exemptions which have made the tax system ever more inefficient.

The biggest items are: reducing tax exemptions on Sunday, holiday and night work; tightening up on opportunities for companies to divert funds to reserves; cutting personal travel allowances and halving the tax-free interest income allowance.
More coalition wrangling can be expected on the VAT issue, with Waigel favouring a one-point increase in the 15 percent rate to balance out his tax arithmetic.

But Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) are badly split on the issue. Regional leaders -- worried about upcoming elections -- oppose a hike while most leaders at party headquarters want a two-point hike to bail out the German social security system.

Coalition agreement on the tax front will end the first chapter in a lengthy consultation process which will involve Germany's regional states and other bodies before legislation is introduced to parliament.
The SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, has already said it would use its veto in the Bundesrat to block a VAT increase.
